content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a method to bound the count of the number of linear regions in sparse neural network models. The authors claim to show results on a tiny (20x20) fully-connected MNIST model that show a correlation between generalization, sparsity ("density") and the bounds on counts of linear regions, and propose that sparsity affects the number of linear regions in a NN. The authors suggest their method can be used to determine better pruning rates.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
* As far as I know there is no previous work explicitly looking at the number of linear regions in the functions learned by sparse neural networks, and their relationship to generalization/sparsity. Addressed properly, this could be an area of interest to the sparse neural network research community.
* Impressive and comprehensive list of references within the area of sparse training and pruning, and likely within the linear regions literature as well. 
* The authors appear to extend existing methods of counting linear regions in order to count the linear regions within a sparse model.

# Weaknesses
* The elephant in the room is the possibly trivial relationship, or at least very strong correlation, of the number of linear regions to model capacity and the fact that of course model capacity varies with sparsity! The authors do not address this or capacity explicitly at all in their paper. 
* Unclear motivation, it seems like the authors are proposing that a correlation between # linear regions and generalization can predict how much we could prune a model, and in the context of counting the linear regions in a dense model this might make sense, but their analysis is as far as I can tell on sparse models.
* Hard paper to read, with large sections of the paper reading like a thought experiment rather than concise explanation or derivation of the method. While I appreciate the author's want to explain their reasoning in their method for counting linear regions, this is much too verbose, and hard to follow because of that.
* Undecipherable results which are only presented in Figures 1-3 (see quality discussion for many details on the figures front),  and no meaningful discussion of results. Results have no obvious link to sparsity/density, and it even being unclear if accuracy is training/generalization is presented. Results also don't appear to give the results the authors claim, but it's just simply hard to tell what they show to begin with.
* Results only demonstrated on tiny (under-capacity) fully-connected neural networks on MNIST. This is likely necessary due to the expense of counting linear regions, but its far from clear that under-capacity models have anything to tell us about optimization of sparse models in general when they are under-parameterized already. In a small MNIST model (e.g. 20x20 neurone as used in the author's experiments) we already have little excess capacity, and are likely under-capacity. What does the author's proposed method tell us when there is only 4 parameters total in layer 2 of their models (which would occur at 99% sparsity for their model), and is this meaningful when we know we can't possibly solve MNIST with such a model?
* Multiple times authors mention expense of calculating linear regions is expensive, but do not quantify this. It is of interest as they are promoting their method of counting linear regions as a way of diagnosing issues with pruning, but it seems this is infeasible computationally on practical models.
* The general motivation is bizarre, at least from a sparse neural network researcher's viewpoint, the authors state: "one question keeps pushing this area: how can we get away with more neural network pruning"? Reading this as higher pruning/more sparsity, this is not in fact close to the most pressing question in the sparse neural network community, in fact I would say more commonly researchers are surprised at just how extreme a sparsity allows good generalization, as there are of course lower bounds to the number of parameters/capacity we need to learn a function!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is unfortunately of low quality in both the presentation of the work, organization of the paper and readability. In particular the few figures of results that are presented are hard to understand having no labels, in some cases no descriptions of the axis in the caption, and poor captions/descriptions. In terms of repeatability, although we are made aware that linear regions are counted using a linear solver, we are not given code of pseudo-code for this as far as I can tell, and this is core to the contributions of the paper.

Further details on the undecipherable results figures:
* No obvious link of curves in figures 1-3 to sparsity/density (in fact we are told in the figure the density is varied and the same between the layers, but we are never given a concrete density or density range! We are simply told "the same density p is used in both layers".
* Figures use multiple y-axis, and do not give axis labels anywhere. In fact I can't figure out what the left y-axis on Figure 1/2 is even in reading the caption/paper.
* It's not clear what "mean accuracy" presented in the results is, is it training, test, or validation accuracy

content.title: Main response
content.comment:
We appreciate the detailed response from the reviewer. We believe that some points about our work were not sufficiently clear, and we provide below as much detail as possible regarding the points that you have raised. If they satisfy your concerns, we will update the paper accordingly.

We address your specific comments in separate messages below.

content.title: Points 1, 2, and 3
content.comment:
> *The elephant in the room is the possibly trivial relationship, or at least very strong correlation, of the number of linear regions to model capacity and the fact that of course model capacity varies with sparsity! The authors do not address this or capacity explicitly at all in their paper.*

Indeed, we cannot rule out this possibility. However, the number of linear regions is an approach to evaluate model expressiveness that has been extensively studied, and also successfully applied as a criterion for neural architecture search in the literature. By extending the current theory of linear regions to the case in which the neural network is sparse, we gain insight on the extent to which pruning does not affect this particular metric, and we find it insightful that pruning affects the upper bound of the number of linear regions in a similar way to which it affects the accuracy of the model.

> *Unclear motivation, it seems like the authors are proposing that a correlation between # linear regions and generalization can predict how much we could prune a model, and in the context of counting the linear regions in a dense model this might make sense, but their analysis is as far as I can tell on sparse models.*

That is actually an interesting point: in dense models, pruning has little to no effect on accuracy, and likewise we see little to no effect on the upper bound for the number of linear regions. Therefore, for both metrics it is only when the model gets sufficiently sparse that we start to see an effect. For that reason, we do not believe that it would be useful to study networks that remain sufficiently dense. In fact, the pruning literature is mostly concerned with making the models as lean and sparse as possible.

> *Hard paper to read, with large sections of the paper reading like a thought experiment rather than concise explanation or derivation of the method. While I appreciate the author's want to explain their reasoning in their method for counting linear regions, this is much too verbose, and hard to follow because of that.*

Following what we have observed as good practice in the deep learning literature, we tried to keep the paper as approachable as possible. We wanted to help the readers understand as much as possible about the elements leading to some architectures being more expressive than others. That led to pushing the proof of the theorem to the appendix, where we formally discuss how we obtained our results.

content.title: Author Rebuttal
content.comment:
I'd like to thank the authors for their rebuttal, and the significant effort they put into responding to my comments. My apologies for my late reply in the discussion period. I found the author's comments interesting, although overall I would not change my rating significantly as there are just too many questions remaining on the relationship between capacity, linear regions and sparsity that arise in the motivation and results of this work in the context of tiny MNIST models that are necessary to address. Furthermore, there are outstanding issues with the presentation of the results and a lack of experimental details preventing repeatability of the work.

## Point 1/Point 2:

As the authors point out, much sparsity research is motivated by the empirical result that apparently model capacity (or at least generalization) is not significantly reduced in some forms of sparse training, and arguably pruning methods. However, typically the models that do not suffer in generalization are *much* larger than those looked at in this work. Perhaps the main issue I have with the empirical results in this paper is that the models used are so small, that they are already in a constrained regime where sparsity doesn't work very well empirically, and I'm quite sure the models are of much lower capacity emperically at any significant level of sparsity. I appreciate in particular the authors explanation that not all layers are pruned to the same sparsity level (I didn't find this clear in the original text), but even neglecting this, these models are just too small to be pruned effectively (i.e. maintain generalization at high sparsity).

## Point 2:
On the verbosity of the paper, I would definitely lean towards making the paper understandable always, but long-winded explanations can also be less understandable than more concise explanations.

content.title: Point 4
content.comment:
> *Undecipherable results which are only presented in Figures 1-3 (see quality discussion for many details on the figures front), and no meaningful discussion of results. Results have no obvious link to sparsity/density, and it even being unclear if accuracy is training/generalization is presented. Results also don't appear to give the results the authors claim, but it's just simply hard to tell what they show to begin with.*

Fig 1 shows the comparison between the mean test accuracy for 30 models (represented by the blue curve and the right y axis) and the log base 2 of the mean number of linear regions for 30 models (represented by the olive curve and the left y axis) on the affine subspace defined by S = 2, 3, 5 sample points when the same density p is used in both layers. As discussed in the paper, we counted the number of linear regions in these networks by restricting the input to the affine space defined by 2, 3, and 5 sample points randomly chosen from the dataset, which respectively define subspaces with dimension at most 1, 2, and 4.

Fig 2 uses almost the same components as Fig1, but instead of using the log base 2 of the mean number of linear regions for 30 models, we use the log base 2 of the upper bound obtained from theorem 1.

Both Fig 1 and Fig 2 suggest a correlation between the theory of linear regions and the accuracy of the pruned model. Working on that, we devised the experiments aiming to capture the correlation between the upper bound of linear regions and the test accuracy of Perceptron 100x100, 200x200, 400x400 and LeNet on MNIST, CIFAR10, and FashionMNIST.

Fig 3 shows the comparison between mean test accuracy (y-axis)  for 30 models trained and then pruned with a density p (a-xis) when (i) the same density is used in all layers (blue curve); and (ii) the density is chosen to increase the bound from Theorem 1 (orange curve). The bar chart shows the difference in the test accuracy between the models in (ii) and (i). A positive value suggests that the test accuracy of models in (ii) is greater than that of models in (i). 

Looking at the charts for MNIST, CIFAR10, and FashionMNIST, we see that models in (ii) outperforms the models in (i) in the majority of the time. This suggests that with more of the upper bound being preserved, we can maintain higher accuracy for models even at lower densities.

content.title: Author Rebuttal
content.comment:
## Point 4

I'm still unclear as to what the x-axis is then? Is it density/sparsity? Graphs/plots should always have all axis clearly labelled. All of these details should be incorporated into the figures themselves in any future revision by the authors.  

It is well known that using dual-axis plots with arbitrary scales can easily mislead on the relationship between two quantities, and should always be avoided. This is especially the case when the zero baselines do not correspond as in the plots presented here. It would be a mistake to read too much into the plots in figure 1/2 for this reason alone.

content.title: Points 5, 6, and 7
content.comment:
> *Results only demonstrated on tiny (under-capacity) fully-connected neural networks on MNIST. This is likely necessary due to the expense of counting linear regions, but its far from clear that under-capacity models have anything to tell us about optimization of sparse models in general when they are under-parameterized already. In a small MNIST model (e.g. 20x20 neurone as used in the author's experiments) we already have little excess capacity, and are likely under-capacity. What does the author's proposed method tell us when there is only 4 parameters total in layer 2 of their models (which would occur at 99% sparsity for their model), and  is this meaningful when we know we can't possibly solve MNIST with such a model?*

While we do study the number of linear regions on subspaces of the input of trained networks, our approach towards pruning is based on our proposed upper bound on their number of linear regions. Because for the same sparsity we can prune more from one layer and less from another, we can use the upper bound for choosing per-layer pruning rates that have a less effect on the upper bound. The smaller a layer is, the less the method would tell us to prune it, as the pruned weight matrices in small layers would be more likely to decrease their rank, causing a loss in dimension and thus reducing the upper bound of the # of linear regions. The method prioritizes pruning from largerlayers as they have larger weight matrices, thus being better at preserving their ranks.
Given actual numbers, a 20x20 layer has a first layer weight matrix of 784x20 (in the case of MNIST). Pruning 99% doesn’t mean we are just pruning the second layer 20X20 connections. Our algorithm instead potentially prunes more from the first layer, preserving a reasonable portion of the second layer. As such, the model will retain as many neurons as possible to solve MNIST and other problems.

> *Multiple times authors mention expense of calculating linear regions is expensive, but do not quantify this. It is of interest as they are promoting their method of counting linear regions as a way of diagnosing issues with pruning, but it seems this is infeasible computationally on practical models.*

As mentioned previously, our approach towards pruning is focused on the upper bound, and as such it does not require counting all the linear regions of the network.

> *The general motivation is bizarre, at least from a sparse neural network researcher's viewpoint, the authors state: "one question keeps pushing this area: how can we get away with more neural network pruning"? Reading this as higher pruning/more sparsity, this is not in fact close to the most pressing question in the sparse neural network community, in fact I would say more commonly researchers are surprised at just how extreme a sparsity allows good generalization, as there are of course lower bounds to the number of parameters/capacity we need to learn a function!*

It is indeed surprising how much we can prune from a neural network, but it remains a central pursuit in the literature to figure out ways to prune even more. The success of a pruning algorithm relies on pruning more for the same accuracy or pruning the same with better accuracy. And this is exactly what we are proposing here: a method based on the theory of linear regions that allows us to prune more than it would be possible if we were to prune the same amount from each layer.

content.title: Author Rebuttal
content.comment:
## Point 5:

I appreciate the clarification that the sparsity varies by layer, but all of these details should be in the paper. I looked through the paper and can't find the details on the sparsity used for each layer in the models looked at. There are very few experimental details overall, and without these the experiments are simply not repeatable.

## Point 6:

Likely I misunderstood here, and I appreciate the clarification. Still, it's obvious there is something limiting your empirical analysis to very small models, is this not the compute required to approximate the upper bound on the number of linear regions?

## Point 7:

I think pruning more for the same generalization is a much better wording to motivate the work to the sparsity community, but understanding optimization and capacity/representational power is also of interest to the community alone.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper uses the theory of linear regions to motivate how to prune. In particular, the authors prove an upper bound on the expected number of linear regions in a ReLU network and then show through experiments on MNIST with small networks that accuracy and number of linear regions (estimated using a few sample points) are closely correlated. Moreover, through their experiments they also show that the derived upper bound also closely correlates with the accuracy. The final section of the paper shows how varying the amount of pruning across layers to maximize the upper bound on the expected number of linear regions can be used to prune more effectively i.e. achieve better accuracy with equal number of parameters.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper invents a new method for network pruning inspired by the theory of linear regions. According to its basic assumption, a network represents a piecewise linear function where the number of pieces is related to accuracy and sparsity. The authors prove an upper bound on the expected number of linear regions to guide the weight matrices pruning for certain sparsity. Moreover, this also reveals how the network represents the knowledge learned inside, which is beneficial for interpretation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ The idea of this paper is new and inspiring. This is a pioneering work to apply the theory of linear regions for network pruning which is convincing and promising.

+ This paper has proved an upper bound to estimate the number of linear regions that is helpful for guide network pruning.

+ The discussion of related works are comprehensive to cover most of the related literature. 

Cons:
- As discussed in the paper, the existing works have already applied the theory of linear regions to measure the network's capacity for universal learning. This paper seems to be the one extending this theory to a sub-area for pruning.

- This paper seems not to be well prepared. All the experiments are conducted over the MNIST, which is too simple and not convincing. I strongly recommend the authors try larger datasets such as ImageNet.

- Some important baselines are missing. [1] and [2] investigated a similar topic of how much to prune. These should be included for comparison of discussion.

[1] Channel Pruning for Accelerating Very Deep Neural Networks. ICCV 17

[2] Learning Structured Sparsity in Deep Neural Networks. NeurIPS 16

content.title: Main response
content.comment:
We appreciate the candid but very encouraging remarks from the reviewer. One point we would like to emphasize is that, to the best of our knowledge, this is first time that the theory of linear regions is applied for actionable insights. Furthermore, network pruning is very vibrant area, but one in which the theoretical understanding is yet not as extensive.

We address your specific comments in separate messages below.

content.title: Points 1, 2, and 3
content.comment:
> *As discussed in the paper, the existing works have already applied the theory of linear regions to measure the network's capacity for universal learning. This paper seems to be the one extending this theory to a sub-area for pruning.*

It is true that we are extending the theory of linear regions to pruning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bridge the gap between pruning and linear regions by presenting an actionable use of that theoretical framework. This is also a convenient application given the lack of theoretical understanding behind network pruning. 

> *This paper seems not to be well prepared. All the experiments are conducted over the MNIST, which is too simple and not convincing. I strongly recommend the authors try larger datasets such as ImageNet.*

While we have restricted our experiment on counting linear regions on subspaces to MNIST, the most important experiments in the paper - those connecting the upper bounds with pruning - were performed on three different datasets. We are working on obtaining results with larger networks and more complex datasets, and we will update our response if we succeed.

> *Some important baselines are missing. [1] and [2] investigated a similar topic of how much to prune. These should be included for comparison of discussion.*

We will include those references in our discussion. Our method could be considered complementary to commonly used pruning methods by leveraging the theory of linear regions to guide such methods on how to prune more or less from each layer.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5630 by Reviewer nY49

content.title: Main response
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer's reasonably positive assessment of our work. Our intent was to extend the theory of linear regions in a direction that could lead to actionable insights, which is the case of network pruning. We note that the peer reviewed literature on liner regions mainly deals with fully-connected feedforward networks. We too would like to extend this work to more complex architectures, and we believe that this initial step of using that theory for the case of network pruning might be an encouragement for further work in this topic.

We address your specific comments in separate messages below.

content.title: Point 1, 2, and 3
content.comment:
> *The title of this work is "getting away with more network pruning", but the final findings can only be applied on fully connected layers, I think it overclaimed its contributions.*

We made our best attempt to capture our contribution in the title while keeping it concise. Our work captures a phenomenon that is more relevant in the context of fully connected layers, which is where we expect it to have the most impact. However, we describe in Appendix C how this could also impact convolutional layers - although to a lesser extent.

> *It's good to see this work give enough theoretical analysis. But more experimental results should be given to prove the effects of the finds of how much to prune from each layer, not just on MNIST/CIFAR on the very small neural network like LeNet.*

We agree with your suggestion. We are working on obtaining results with larger networks and more complex datasets, and we will update our response if we succeed.

> *Currently, the connections between the upper bound and network accuracy under pruning can only be used to prune fully connected layers, which limits the application of these findings. Actually, convolutional neural networks (ConvNet) and Self-attention neural networks (Transformer) are both special cases of fc layers. The kernel of ConvNet has shared fc parameters and self-attention is purely based on fc with matrix operation and softmax. Can the proof and finds in this work be also applied to ConvNet and Transformer?*

As previously mentioned, while the findings are also applicable to convolutional layers, we expect less impact in that particular case due to the reasons mentioned in Appendix C. Regarding transformers, most SOTA architectures use GeLU instead of ReLU. As GeLU is not a piecewise linear activation function, we cannot apply the same method to models using GeLU as its activation function. The same applies to softmax. However, due to the considerable use of ReLU and other piecewise linear activations, better understanding how to prune networks with such activations remains relevant.

content.comment:
Thanks for the response from the authors. 
I appreciate the explanations for each of my concens, and some of my expected results are not given in the response. I keep my score.
